title: Rapid Response Team (RRT) Activation
summary: Recognizing early clinical deterioration and activating the rapid response team before cardiac arrest occurs.
steps: Recognize early warning signs of deterioration (any of the following):
HR <40 or >130 bpm
RR <8 or >28 breaths/min
SpO2 <90% on supplemental O2
Systolic BP <90 mmHg
Acute change in level of consciousness
Urine output <50mL over 4 hours
Acute, uncontrolled pain
Staff or family 'gut feeling' that something is wrong
CALL THE RAPID RESPONSE TEAM: activate per facility protocol (usually dedicated RRT number or call overhead).
Stay with patient. Send someone else to call if needed.
While awaiting RRT: apply O2, obtain vital signs, establish IV access if not present.
Prepare SBAR: Situation (what's wrong), Background (history/admitting diagnosis), Assessment (vital signs, clinical findings), Recommendation (what you need).
Gather: chart, medication list, allergies, code status, provider contact info.
Document: time of deterioration first noticed, interventions prior to RRT arrival, RRT team members.
safetyTips: Calling RRT is NEVER wrong if you are concerned. Under-calling leads to preventable codes.
RRT activation is not a personal failure — it is the correct clinical decision.
Document the time you first noticed deterioration — this is critical for incident review.
keyTakeaways: Any nurse can and should call RRT

title: Sepsis Recognition & Hour-1 Bundle
summary: Recognizing sepsis and initiating the Surviving Sepsis Campaign Hour-1 Bundle.
equipment: IV fluid (30mL/kg NS or LR bolus)
steps: SCREEN for sepsis: suspected infection + ≥2 SIRS criteria (HR>90, RR>20, Temp>38°C or <36°C, WBC>12K or <4K) OR using qSOFA (≥2 of: altered mental status, RR≥22, SBP≤100).
HOUR-1 BUNDLE (Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2018):
1. Measure lactate (target <2 mmol/L; re-measure if >2 mmol/L after resuscitation).
2. Blood cultures BEFORE antibiotics (2 sets from different sites — do not delay antibiotics >45 min for cultures).
3. Broad-spectrum antibiotics within 1 hour of sepsis recognition.
4. 30 mL/kg IV crystalloid bolus for hypotension (SBP<90 or MAP<65) or lactate ≥4 mmol/L.
5. Vasopressors if MAP <65 after fluid resuscitation (norepinephrine is first-line; via central line preferred).
Monitor response: MAP, urine output, lactate clearance, mental status.
Reassess fluid responsiveness — avoid fluid overload in patients without response (consider passive leg raise test).
safetyTips: Do NOT delay antibiotics waiting for cultures — each hour of delay increases mortality by ~7%.
Septic shock vasopressors via peripheral IV temporarily acceptable if central line not available.
Lactate ≥4 mmol/L = septic shock even without hypotension — initiate bundle immediately.
documentation: Blood culture draw times and sites
keyTakeaways: Hour-1 bundle: lactate, cultures, antibiotics, fluids, vasopressors

title: Stroke Recognition & Assessment (BE-FAST / NIH Stroke Scale)
summary: Rapidly recognizing stroke symptoms, completing the NIH Stroke Scale, and activating the stroke response.
steps: RECOGNIZE with BE-FAST:
B — Balance: sudden loss of balance or coordination
E — Eyes: sudden vision changes
F — Face: facial drooping (ask patient to smile)
A — Arm: arm weakness (ask patient to hold arms up)
S — Speech: slurred or strange speech (ask to repeat a phrase)
T — Time: note exact time of symptom onset (or last-known-well)
ACTIVATE STROKE CODE: notify provider and stroke team IMMEDIATELY.
Check blood glucose — hypoglycemia mimics stroke. If <60 mg/dL, treat first.
Obtain IV access. NPO. Do NOT give food or fluids (dysphagia risk).
Complete NIHSS (scored 0–42): consciousness, gaze, visual fields, facial palsy, motor arm/leg, limb ataxia, sensory, language, dysarthria, extinction.
Obtain stat CT head without contrast (rules out hemorrhage before tPA).
tPA (alteplase) time window: 3–4.5 hours from symptom onset. Document last-known-well time precisely.
BP management: keep BP <185/110 before tPA. Do not treat BP aggressively unless ≥220/120 and tPA not planned.
safetyTips: TIME IS BRAIN: 1.9 million neurons die per minute during stroke. Speed is critical.
Never give tPA without CT confirming no hemorrhage.
Correct last-known-well time is crucial — patient waking with symptoms = time was at sleep.
documentation: tPA administration or reason not given

title: Trauma Primary Survey (ABCDE)
summary: Performing the ATLS-based primary survey to identify and treat immediately life-threatening injuries.
steps: GENERAL IMPRESSION: mechanism of injury, visible hemorrhage, level of consciousness.
A — AIRWAY with cervical spine protection: is airway patent? Jaw thrust (not chin-lift) if trauma. Apply c-collar. If obstructed: suction, airway adjunct, prepare for intubation.
B — BREATHING & VENTILATION: RR, SpO2, tracheal deviation, breath sounds. Apply 100% O2 NRB. Tension pneumothorax: absent breath sounds + tracheal deviation + hypotension — needle decompression STAT.

C — CIRCULATION & HEMORRHAGE CONTROL: HR, BP, skin (pale/cool = shock). Stop external bleeding: direct pressure, tourniquet for extremity. Start 2 large-bore IVs. Warm crystalloid 1–2L (consider early blood products).
D — DISABILITY (NEUROLOGICAL STATUS): GCS, pupils (PERRLA), focal deficits. Check glucose.
E — EXPOSURE & ENVIRONMENT: fully expose patient to find all injuries. Log roll to assess back. Cover with warm blanket immediately to prevent hypothermia.
ADJUNCTS: cardiac monitor, 12-lead ECG, foley if no urethral injury, NG tube if no facial fractures, portable X-rays (chest, pelvis), FAST ultrasound.
Transition to secondary survey (head-to-toe) once life threats addressed.
safetyTips: Hypothermia + acidosis + coagulopathy = the lethal trauma triad. Prevent with warming, early blood products, damage control.
Tension pneumothorax: do NOT wait for X-ray. Clinical diagnosis — needle decompression immediately.
Tourniquet for uncontrolled extremity hemorrhage. Document application time — ischemic risk >2 hours.
keyTakeaways: Stop the bleeding — hemorrhage is the #1 preventable death

title: Anaphylaxis Recognition & Emergency Management
summary: Recognizing and managing anaphylaxis, a life-threatening systemic allergic reaction.
steps: RECOGNIZE: rapid onset of ≥2 body systems after allergen exposure:
Skin: hives, flushing, angioedema (lips/tongue/throat)
Respiratory: bronchospasm, stridor, hypoxia
Cardiovascular: hypotension, tachycardia, dizziness
GI: nausea, vomiting, abdominal cramping
CALL FOR HELP. Activate rapid response / code as appropriate.
EPINEPHRINE FIRST — 0.3mg (0.3mL of 1:1000) IM into outer mid-thigh. This is the primary treatment. Do NOT delay.
Repeat epinephrine every 5–15 minutes if needed. Up to 3 doses.
Position: supine with legs elevated (unless respiratory distress — then semi-Fowler).
Apply high-flow O2 via NRB mask. Be prepared for intubation (airway edema can close rapidly).
IV access: large bore ×2. NS bolus 1–2L for hypotension.
Secondary medications (AFTER epinephrine): diphenhydramine 50mg IV/IM, methylprednisolone 125mg IV, albuterol for bronchospasm.
Monitor for biphasic reaction (symptom return 1–72 hours later) — observe minimum 4–8 hours post-reaction.
safetyTips: Epinephrine is the ONLY first-line treatment — antihistamines alone will NOT reverse anaphylaxis.
Angioedema of the airway can close within minutes. Have intubation equipment at bedside.
Biphasic reaction occurs in up to 20% — do not discharge immediately after initial stabilization.

title: Arterial Blood Gas (ABG) Collection
summary: Collecting an arterial blood gas sample from the radial artery and interpreting the results.
equipment: Ice bag (for transport if delay >15 min)
steps: Verify order. Perform Allen's test to assess collateral circulation:
Compress both radial and ulnar arteries. Have patient clench fist until blanched.
Release ulnar artery only. Hand should flush pink within 5–6 seconds. >10 seconds = inadequate collateral circulation. Choose another site.
Position wrist in extension (rolled towel under wrist).
Perform hand hygiene. Don gloves.
Clean radial pulse with alcohol swab. Allow to dry.
Palpate radial artery with non-dominant index finger.
Insert needle bevel up at 30–45° angle over pulsation. Advance slowly — blood will flash back under arterial pressure (pulsatile).
Allow 0.5–1 mL to fill (gravity/pulsatile — do not pull back on plunger).
Withdraw needle. Apply firm pressure for minimum 5 minutes (10 minutes if anticoagulated).
Expel air bubbles from syringe immediately. Cap the syringe. Label and transport to lab (or on ice if >15 minute delay).
safetyTips: Pressure is critical — arterial hematomas can be large. Do not release pressure early.
If patient is on anticoagulation (heparin, warfarin) hold pressure for 10–15 minutes minimum.
Air bubbles in the syringe falsely normalize PaO2 and PaCO2 — expel immediately.
documentation: O2 therapy and FiO2 at time of sample
